splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects how courts handle revocation proceedings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for tolling supervised release during absconding, and the term runs regardless of the supervisee's compliance.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars raising any previously presented claim — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter bar than Congress may have intended; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of new evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on relitigating previously presented claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, requiring only that they satisfy § 2255(h)'s conditions of new evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures like mail-in ballot deadlines. The outcome determines whether such challenges can proceed before an election or must wait until after votes are cast, with significant implications for election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws before an election based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful voting procedures.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge state election laws pre-election because the alleged injury from counting late-arriving ballots is too speculative.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency/Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations in the criminal sentencing context. At least three circuits hold lenity prevails, while the Third Circuit has held that deference trumps lenity. The issue is especially important after the Supreme Court overruled Chevron in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in the criminal context, requiring ambiguities to be resolved in the defendant's favor.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary takes priority over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions in the criminal context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the Guidelines text after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' under the career-offender guideline is entitled to deference after Kisor. Some circuits continue to defer, while others hold the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. This split affects thousands of career-offender designations annually.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a permissible interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses under § 4B1.2.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can be considered as a factor contributing to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law — particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive 'stacked' § 924(c) sentences — when evaluating compassionate release motions. Some circuits permit consideration of such changes as one factor among others, while others categorically bar it. This split affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences that would be dramatically lower under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as contributing to extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled, or whether a state conviction involving any state-controlled substance qualifies. The split affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-schedule requirement
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal-schedule requirement applies
positions.summary: Holds that a state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, applying a categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment order (attorney's fees in criminal cases) is governed by the civil 30-day deadline or the criminal 14-day deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case — triggering the longer 30-day appeal deadline — or a criminal matter governed by the shorter 14-day deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view applying the civil deadline, but noted this is a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline (30 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and the 30-day civil appeal deadline applies.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Trident Seafoods Corp.

positions.label: Criminal deadline (14 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises from and is part of the criminal case, and the shorter criminal appeal deadline applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 is available to challenge conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement), or whether prisoners must use civil rights actions (Bivens or § 1983) for such claims.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is available only to challenge the fact or duration of confinement, or also extends to challenges to conditions of confinement, including BOP decisions about First Step Act time credits and transfer to prerelease custody. The split affects the remedies available to thousands of federal prisoners seeking to enforce statutory rights.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus may be used to challenge conditions and terms of confinement, not only the fact or duration of imprisonment, including BOP decisions about earned time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy only for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, and that other challenges must be brought through civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may impose sentences at supervised release revocation that expressly punish defendants for the underlying violation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit permits courts to expressly punish defendants for the underlying violation conduct, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences may only address the breach of the court's trust, not punish the new conduct. This affects hundreds of revocation proceedings annually.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct is permitted
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying a supervised release violation when imposing a revocation sentence.

positions.label: Revocation addresses breach of trust only
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of a revocation sentence is to sanction the breach of the court's trust inherent in the violation, not to punish the underlying criminal conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination in the operation of hospitality or business establishments, and what remedies are available under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 for such claims?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, suggesting the existence of a circuit split or unsettled question about how courts evaluate fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages in the hospitality and service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, potentially allowing claims based on differential treatment without requiring a comparator or direct evidence of racial animus.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring stronger showings of discriminatory intent or use of comparator evidence to establish discrimination claims in business establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption provision — which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any . . . broker' — preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries caused by motor carriers they selected. This affects tort liability across the trucking industry.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that the FAAAA preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers because such claims are 'related to' the broker's services.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that common-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are too attenuated from the broker's prices, routes, or services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence — claims that might also be raised under § 2255 — as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts evaluating compassionate release motions may consider arguments that overlap with habeas-type claims challenging the validity of the underlying conviction or sentence. Some circuits permit such considerations as part of the totality of circumstances, while others hold these claims must be channeled exclusively through habeas proceedings.

positions.label: May consider habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider arguments about potential errors in the conviction or sentence as part of the compassionate release analysis, even if those claims could also be raised in a § 2255 motion.

positions.label: May not consider habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release is not an appropriate vehicle for challenging the validity of a conviction or sentence, and such claims must be raised exclusively through habeas proceedings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
